extracted.intended_audience: trial judges and patent litigators (counsel) in U.S. patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials in U.S. federal courts that provide judges and counsel with neutral, customizable language and legal standards on claim construction, infringement, invalidity, damages, willfulness, and related procedural matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of neutral, case-specific jury instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the fundamental goals of the Instructions is to provide a neutral set of jury instructions that would not be biased in favor of either the patent owner or the accused infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions are not intended to address every conceivable issue; litigants must tailor these Instructions to the specific issues in their case and eliminate superfluous or confusing instructions. Bracketed terminology is used so parties can find-and-replace case-specific facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary instructions and trial procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the jury: Now that you have been sworn, I have the following preliminary instructions for your guidance on the nature of the case and on your role as jurors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain phases of a jury trial (selection, opening statements, evidence, closing arguments, final instructions, deliberations); opening and closing statements are not evidence; deposition testimony is entitled to same consideration as live testimony; keep open mind until all evidence is heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and purpose of patents and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent gives the owner the right to exclude others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention within the United States or importing it into the United States. The specification should have a written description of the invention, how it works, and how to make and use it so as to enable others skilled in the art. The claims define the scope of the patent owner’s exclusive rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide jurors background on patent prosecution, Office Actions, and the prosecution history (file wrapper); clarify that only claims can be infringed, not the written description or drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof for infringement (preponderance)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Plaintiff] must prove that [the Defendant] infringes one or more claims ... by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preponderance of the evidence is described as slightly greater than 50%; apply this standard to infringement and most other issues except invalidity (clear and convincing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and standard for invalidity (clear and convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is presumed to be valid. To overcome the presumption of validity, [the Defendant] must prove invalidity of each challenged claim by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note suggests substituting or explaining 'clear and convincing' as 'highly probable' to aid juror understanding; explains relationship between evidence standards (preponderance < clear-and-convincing < beyond a reasonable doubt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of the jury's main issues (post-trial verdict)
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury must decide: (1) whether [the Plaintiff] has proven that [the Defendant] infringed asserted claims; (2) whether [the Defendant] has proven that asserted claims are invalid; (3) what amount of damages, if any, [the Plaintiff] has proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List any other patent issues to be decided; instruct jury that issues are typically decided claim-by-claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — judge provides meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the judge's job to provide to the jury the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted. Jurors must accept the meanings given and use them for both infringement and invalidity decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For limitations not construed by the court, use the plain and ordinary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention. Cite relevant authority (Phillips, Teva).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-/step-plus-function claim construction (§ 112 ¶6 / §112(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim element is in the form of a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function, the element is interpreted to cover only the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge determines the recited function and corresponding structure/steps; Instruction 2.2 recommended where means/step language is used to avoid jury confusion; include statutory and case citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement assessed claim-by-claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is assessed claim-by-claim. Defendant may infringe some claims but not others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare accused product/method to the patent claims (not to the patentee's commercial product); distinguish literal infringement from doctrine of equivalents and direct from indirect infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement — each claim element present
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the Defendant's product/method includes each and every element/method step in that patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the accused product/method does not contain one or more elements/steps, it does not literally infringe that claim; determine literal infringement for each asserted claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — equivalence for missing elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is infringed under the doctrine of equivalents only if there is an equivalent component/part/method step in the accused product/method for each element/method step of the patent claim that is not literally present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that accused product contains equivalents for each missing element; practice notes discuss limits (e.g., prosecution history estoppel, dedication to the public).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement — knowledge and intent immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement is established by acts that fall within the scope of the claims; knowledge of the patent and intent to infringe are immaterial to direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate instructions exist for literal infringement, joint infringement, means-plus-function literal infringement, and infringement of dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Special instructions govern joint infringement where multiple actors perform claim steps such that one actor can be held responsible for the actions of others under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the legal standard and guidance applicable to joint performance of claim steps (the instruction set contains a dedicated section).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of means-plus-function or step-plus-function claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Literal infringement of means-plus-function or step-plus-function claims requires that the accused device or process contain the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification or equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the court's construction of the means/step element (see Instruction 2.2); jurors must be instructed on corresponding structure or steps identified in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement of dependent claims is evaluated by comparing the accused product/method to the dependent claim language which incorporates limitations of an earlier claim and adds further limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss how dependent claims relate to independent claims and how infringement is determined for dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim language constructions for 'comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of'
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions include guidance on infringement analyses for claims using transitional or limitative claim language such as 'comprising of', 'consisting of', and 'consisting essentially of'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the legal effect of those transitional phrases on claim scope and infringement findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — active inducement
rubrics_metrics.description: Active inducement of patent infringement requires proof that the defendant induced another to infringe the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate instructions for induced infringement and contributory infringement (including factual and intent elements) and distinctions from direct infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory infringement involves supplying a component especially made or adapted for use in a patented invention knowing it to be especially made or adapted and not a staple article suitable for substantial noninfringing use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes statutory references and guidance distinguishing contributory infringement from other forms and including 271(f) and 271(g) contexts when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by supply of components abroad (§ 271(f)(1) and § 271(f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions cover infringement by supplying all or a substantial portion of components of a patented invention to another country (§ 271(f)(1)) and supplying components especially made or adapted for use in a patented invention into another country (§ 271(f)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State statutory standards and case references applying 271(f) doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under § 271(g) — product made by patented process
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement by import, sale, offer for sale, or use of a product made by a patented process is governed by § 271(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide statutory standard and case law guidance for applying § 271(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art — definitions (pre-AIA and AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is defined differently under pre-AIA and AIA: pre-AIA definitions vary by subsection of §102 (e.g., date of invention, one-year bars), while AIA defines prior art as knowledge publicly available before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions include Cutoff Date concepts and Practice Note explaining Cutoff Date may vary by claim and may require jury instructions to determine Cutoff Dates for asserted claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) and its sub-elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation is addressed with instructions on prior public knowledge, prior public use, on-sale bar, experimental use, printed publication, prior patent, and earlier-filed patent application (with pre-AIA and AIA variants where applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each category includes tailored instructions and distinctions between pre-AIA and AIA standards where necessary (e.g., printed publication, prior patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — Graham factors (scope/content of prior art; differences; level of skill; secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness instructions cover: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) other considerations (secondary considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide guidance on how these factors interact; include Practice Notes and case citations; instruct jury on determining person of ordinary skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the level of experience, education, or training generally possessed by those who work in the area of the invention (pre-AIA) or before the effective filing date (AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for claim construction, obviousness, enablement, written description, and other analyses; instructions explain that the level may vary by claim/technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (§ 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe how to make and use the invention in enough detail to enable others skilled in the art to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions include enablement standards and how jurors should evaluate the adequacy of the specification in light of the person of ordinary skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement (§ 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The written-description requirement ensures that the specification adequately describes the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide standards and jury guidance for determining whether specification shows possession of the claimed invention at the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — general principles (§ 284)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages compensate the patent owner for harm caused by infringement. Jury must determine amount of damages, if any, that the Plaintiff has proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions cover starting date for damages, kinds of damages recoverable, burden of proof, and evidentiary considerations; include statutory and case law citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date damages begin — alternate instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide alternative instructions depending on whether the date of the start of the damages period is stipulated or disputed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate A: date stipulated; Alternate B: date disputed — guidance for jurors on determining appropriate start date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of damages recoverable (lost profits, price erosion, cost escalation, convoyed sales, reasonable royalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages may include lost profits, price erosion, cost escalation, convoyed sales, and a reasonable royalty; each category has specific standards for recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed sub-instructions for each damages type (e.g., lost-profits causation, market-share analyses, apportionment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits standard and factors (e.g., Panduit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profits may be recovered where the patent owner proves a causal link between the infringement and lost sales/profits, following applicable legal tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide evidentiary requirements and guidance on calculating lost profits (market demand, causal link, absence of acceptable noninfringing substitutes, and the patent owner's capacity to exploit demand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — hypothetical negotiation (Georgia-Pacific factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is determined by what the parties would have agreed to in a hypothetical negotiation at the time the infringement began; Georgia-Pacific factors may provide a useful framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury may consider comparable licenses, timing, foreseeability, profits, noninfringing substitutes, apportionment, and must account for differences between comparable licenses and the hypothetical license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — timing and foreseeability
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages are based on the hypothetical negotiation at the time of negotiation; evidence need not be limited to facts occurring on or before that date and may include foreseeable or estimated information (post-infringement usage, subsequent licenses, infringer profits) under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn against hindsight; allow consideration of foreseeable post-negotiation evidence when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — availability of non-infringing substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining a reasonable royalty, jurors may consider availability and cost of acceptable non-infringing substitutes to the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute must be licensed under the patent or not infringe the patent; factor into royalty negotiation analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — use of comparable license agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors may consider amounts other parties have paid for rights to the patents or comparable technologies and payment structures; a license need not be perfectly comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on comparable licenses, jurors must account for differences in technologies and economic circumstances when making royalty determinations; cite relevant Federal Circuit authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubts on damages resolved against infringer
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubts the jury may have on damages due to the Defendant’s failure to keep proper records should be decided in favor of the Plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confusion or difficulties caused by the Defendant’s records or lack of records should be held against the Defendant (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) and FRAND considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: For SEPs, Georgia-Pacific factors may be useful, but the jury must be instructed on the particulars of the FRAND commitment and only those relevant Georgia-Pacific factors. Any royalty must be apportioned to the value of the claimed invention (or the approximate value thereof), not the value of the standard as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must be instructed on apportionment and not on irrelevant factors; cite Federal Circuit precedent on SEPs and apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement — totality of circumstances and knowledge/intention
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement is found, the jury must determine whether the infringement was willful. Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that Defendant knew of the patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May consider whether conduct was deliberate or intentional; cannot find willfulness merely because Defendant knew of the patent; consider totality of circumstances at time of challenged conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness — reliance on legal opinion as factor
rubrics_metrics.description: If Defendant relies on counsel’s opinion, jurors may consider whether Defendant reasonably relied on a competent legal opinion as one factor in the willfulness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIA §298 prohibits using failure to obtain an opinion of counsel as evidence of willfulness; instructions should be tailored depending on whether Defendant asserts reliance on counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice Notes and drafting features (bracketed and optional language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice Notes provide guidance and are not meant for jury reading; bracketed terms and double-brackets indicate language to be customized, and alternatives are provided (e.g., [product]/[method], [the Plaintiff]/[the Defendant]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use find-and-replace to insert case-specific facts; remove unnecessary or confusing bracketed alternatives before submitting to jury; Practice Notes aid judges/counsel but are not instructions of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of glossaries for technical and patent terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may prepare and distribute a Glossary of technical terms to jurors to familiarize them with technology and terms used at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model includes a Glossary of Patent Terms and a placeholder for a Glossary of Technical Terms to be agreed upon between parties; use consistent definitions and consider relevance of terms to the case.
